title: Through the Sea on Dry Ground
summary: The LORD turns Israel back to camp by the sea, and Pharaoh, changing his mind, pursues them with his chariots. Trapped between the army and the water, the people panic, but Moses tells them to stand firm and see the LORD's salvation. The LORD divides the sea with a strong east wind, Israel crosses on dry ground, and the returning waters overwhelm the Egyptian army; Israel fears the LORD and believes in him and in Moses.
story: Israel left Egypt in chapter 12 and set out toward the wilderness in chapter 13, led by the pillar of cloud and fire. Now comes the event that the rest of the Bible remembers as the great act of salvation in the Old Testament. The plagues broke Pharaoh's will; the sea breaks his power. Until this chapter Israel has been released; after it, they are rescued, with the enemy gone for good. The crossing marks the boundary between slavery and a new life under God, and it turns a crowd of escaped slaves into a people who have seen what their God can do. In chapter 15 they will sing about it, and for the rest of Scripture the parting of the sea becomes the pattern by which prophets and psalmists describe God rescuing his people (Isaiah 43:16-19; Psalm 77:16-20).
historical:
The date of the exodus is contested (see the note on chapter 13), and so is the place of the crossing. The Hebrew yam suph, rendered Red Sea, literally means sea of reeds, and it is used in the Bible both for the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba (1 Kings 9:26) and possibly for marshy lakes nearer Egypt. Proposed crossing sites include the Gulf of Suez, the Bitter Lakes or Lake Timsah along the line of the modern Suez Canal, a lagoon on the Mediterranean coast, and the Gulf of Aqaba. The place names in verse 2 have not been securely located. Migdol means tower or fort, a common name for Egyptian frontier posts; Baal-zephon is named after a Canaanite god, Baal of the north, whose worship is attested in Egypt's eastern Delta.

The chariot was the elite weapon of New Kingdom Egypt. Egyptian reliefs show light two-wheeled chariots carrying a driver and a warrior, usually an archer, which could run down people on foot in open country. Six hundred chosen chariots, plus the rest, was a formidable force for a people with no army. Historians hold a range of views about the event itself, from those who accept the account as it stands, to those who look for natural processes God used (the text itself names an east wind blowing all night), to those who regard the story as Israel's later, poetic memory of its origins.
cultural:
An ancient reader would have heard this chapter as a clash of gods, not only armies. Pharaoh was regarded as a god on earth, the guarantor of order against chaos, and Egyptian royal art often shows him in his chariot trampling foreign enemies. The sea, across the ancient Near East, was a symbol of chaos, and in Canaanite stories Baal fought the sea god Yam. Here the LORD commands the sea as his servant and uses it to destroy the chariots of the god-king, beside a place named for Baal. The LORD's stated purpose, “I will gain honor by means of Pharaoh”, is a claim about who truly rules.

The night was divided into watches, and the “morning watch” was the last one, before dawn. Soldiers would have expected to attack at first light; instead the Egyptian army is caught in the sea bed in darkness and confusion, with wheels that won't run true. Israel's fear in verses 10-12 reflects the real situation of runaway slaves facing professional troops, and their complaint that there were “no graves in Egypt” carries bitter sarcasm, since Egypt was famous for its tombs.
literary: The chapter is built in three scenes, each opened by a word from the LORD to Moses (verses 1, 15, and 26), and each followed by its fulfillment. It is dense with repetition. The phrase “the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD” returns from the plague chapters (verses 4 and 18). The words “on dry ground, with walls of water on their right and on their left” appear twice (verses 22 and 29), framing the crossing. The pillar moves from before Israel to behind it (verse 19), becoming a wall of darkness and light between the camps. Most striking is how the language of seeing and fearing turns over: Israel sees the Egyptians and fears them (verse 10); Moses says they will see the LORD's salvation and never see the Egyptians again (verse 13); at the end Israel sees the Egyptians dead and fears the LORD (verses 30-31). The story moves the people's fear from the enemy to God.

outline.t: The LORD sets a trap by the sea
Pharaoh changes his mind and pursues
Israel panics; Moses says stand firm
Go forward: the staff raised and the pillar behind
The sea divides and Israel crosses
The waters return, and Israel believes

doctrines.note: The crossing is the Old Testament's model of salvation: a helpless people is rescued by God's action alone. Moses' words, “The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still”, describe rescue as something received, not achieved.

God rules the sea, the wind, and the heart of a king. The chapter speaks both of Pharaoh's own choices (verse 5) and of God hardening his heart (verses 4, 8, 17), holding divine rule and human responsibility together without explaining how.

Faith here grows from seeing what God has done: the people “feared the LORD and believed in Him and in His servant Moses.” Their trust is not yet steady, as the complaints of the coming chapters show, but it is born at the sea.

words.note: Chazaq, to be strong or to make strong. Used of the heart, it means to harden, to make stubborn and resolute. It is one of three verbs Exodus uses for Pharaoh's hardening. In earlier chapters Pharaoh hardens his own heart as well as God hardening it; here God confirms and uses the stubbornness Pharaoh chose, turning it toward its end.

Kavad, to be heavy, and so to be honored or glorified. The LORD says, “I will gain honor by means of Pharaoh.” The same root was used for Pharaoh's heavy, hardened heart in the plague chapters, and here God shows where true weight and glory lie.

Yabbashah, dry land or dry ground. The word first appears in Genesis 1:9-10, where God gathers the waters so the dry land appears. Its use here suggests that the crossing is a new act of creation, God again making dry ground in the midst of the waters for a people he is forming.

Lacham, to fight or wage war. Moses says the LORD will fight for Israel, and the Egyptians themselves concede it: “the LORD is fighting for them against Egypt”. Israel's first battle is one it does not fight at all.

christ: The New Testament reads the crossing as a pattern of the salvation Christ brings. Paul says Israel's ancestors “were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:2), treating the passage through water, under God's presence, as a picture of Christian baptism: passing from bondage into a new life under a new leader. Hebrews lists the crossing as an act of faith (Hebrews 11:29). The exodus shapes the Gospels' language too: in Luke's account of the transfiguration, Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about his departure, and the Greek word Luke uses there is exodos (Luke 9:31). The link is a pattern the New Testament itself draws: as God rescued Israel from slavery through death and water, so in Christ he rescues his people from sin and death, and they receive that rescue rather than earn it.

hard.q: If God hardened Pharaoh's heart, how could Pharaoh be held responsible, and how should we think about the Egyptian soldiers who drowned?
hard.a:
The hardening of Pharaoh is one of the great puzzles of Exodus. Across chapters 4 to 14 the text says both that Pharaoh hardened his own heart and that God hardened it. Some interpreters, often in the Reformed tradition, read this as God's sovereign decree working through Pharaoh's real choices, with no contradiction between them. Others, often in Arminian and some Jewish readings, stress that Pharaoh hardened himself first and that God's hardening was a judicial confirming of the path he had chosen. Both agree that Pharaoh is never pictured as a man who wanted to do right and was prevented. This is a second-order question on which faithful readers differ.

The drowning of the army is harder to feel than to explain. The text presents it as judgment on a regime that had enslaved Israel and ordered the killing of its infant sons, and as the last act of a long contest in which Pharaoh was repeatedly warned. Soldiers are not individually judged; they belong to the power that is destroyed. Later Jewish tradition includes a well-known story in which God rebukes the angels for rejoicing while his creatures drown, and Ezekiel 18:23 insists that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. The Bible celebrates the rescue without asking readers to take pleasure in death.

questions: Israel's fear moves from the Egyptians to the LORD by the end of the chapter. What would it change for you if the fear of God were larger than your other fears?
Moses says, “you need only to be still”, and then God says, “Tell the Israelites to go forward.” How do trust and obedience fit together in hard moments?
The people complain that Egypt would have been better. What past slavery do people sometimes remember more fondly than it deserves?
